newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tourism shrinks Japan trade gap but pace slows.
newsitem.headline: Tourism shrinks Japan trade gap but pace slows.

text.p: Japan's current account surplus, its broadest measure of trade in goods and services, dropped a solid 15.4 percent in November, helped by a surge in spending on trips abroad.
The Finance Ministry announced on Monday that the politically sensitive surplus fell to 664.1 billion yen ($5.72 billion) from 784.9 billion yen ($6.76 billion) in the same month a year earlier.
This was a bigger drop than the six percent dip economists had been anticipating, but the pace of the decline in the surplus was slower than that of the previous month.

Japan's current account surplus has been falling on a year-on-year basis since late 1994, helped by a progessive shift of Japanese manufacturing capacity overseas and by the export-dampening effect of a strong yen. This, and a growing taste for imported goods, has steadily cut back the surplus.

However, a fall in the value of the yen since last year has put the brakes on the trend, raising the possibility of a reversal in the pattern and renewed friction down the road with key trading partners such as the United States.
A weaker yen, although making Japanese exports more competitively priced, can hurt companies with global production bases when they convert their overseas earnings back into yen.

In October, the year-on-year drop in the current account surplus was 19.6 percent, bigger than the November drop of 15.4 percent. The average of forecasts by economists had been for a surplus of 738 billion yen ($6.36 billion) in November.

"It's a little bit better that than what the market was looking for and better for Japan in that the external surplus is still coming down compared to a year ago," said Jesper Koll, head of research at J.P. Morgan in Tokyo.

Akiyoshi Takumori, chief economist at Sakura Securities, said: "The current account surplus is less than what I had expected...It shows that the decreasing trend for the current account is still intact."

The Finance Ministry said the surplus was still declining, albeit at a slower pace, as growth in imports continued to exceed that of exports, and Japan was continuing to run a deficit in services such as tourism.
The deficit in the services balance rose 27 percent to 557.4 billion yen ($4.80 billion) mainly due to an increase in spending by Japanese tourists abroad.

The drop in the trade surplus, a component of the overall current account figure excluding services, was smaller than that of the headline figure -- a mere 3.4 percent year-on-year drop to 859.8 billion yen ($7.41 billion).
The dollar eased slightly on the news of the slowing drop in the current account.
"These figures won't really have much of an impact on the currency market, because they are not so extreme," said Yasuji Yamanaka, vice president at the Bank of America in Tokyo.
"There's the chance that the continuing weakness of the yen will bring us to a point in several months where the decline of the surplus may slow or come to a halt," he said.

This could squeeze U.S. businesses, putting pressure on the U.S. authorities to act, he said. "If this happens, it's hard to know what sort of comments or response we can expect from the U.S. This is something we have to be cautious about, particularly in the currency market."
